title: Chalmers steps in: ATO credit card ban delayed after business uproar
full_text:
The Australian Taxation Office’s controversial banning of credit card payments will no longer come into effect at the end of next month, after the government negotiated with the independent agency to delay the change.
Following an intervention from Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Friday, the government will allocate additional funds to cover the costs of transactions charged to the ATO, while the opposition prepares legislation to block the move entirely.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers. Louie Douvis
“We’ve stepped in to ensure that the tax office can take credit card payments until the end of June next year,” Chalmers said.
“This will give them the time to consult more with small business and to get it right. We try not to interfere with the RBA or the ATO … but it’s really important that we have stepped in today.”
The announcement comes after fierce pushback from the business community, opposition parties and some members of the Labor backbench that saw the ATO’s decision as damaging to the cash-flow management of small businesses. Chalmers said the government took feedback from small business owners very seriously.
Following a review by the Reserve Bank of Australia initiated in 2024, credit card surcharges were banned, and interchange fees lowered, on October 1 of this year. The bank said the combination of moves would have a minimal impact of around 0.1 per cent in consumer costs.
Labor barracked for the change, labelling it cost-of-living support that would lower prices at the checkout. But insiders say the government was blindsided by a move from the ATO to ban credit card payments entirely.
The tax office said it had implemented the ban because the $200 million in associated fees that would now be imposed on its budget was not an appropriate cost to pass on to the taxpayer. The government will provide additional funds to the tax office to extend the transitional period, though the support is expected to be less than $200 million.
Chalmers spoke with tax commissioner Rob Heferen early on Friday morning before briefing government colleagues on the delay. The Treasurer was unable to recall when the government first became aware of the ATO’s credit card ban, but said Labor “insisted” on a transitional period.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor on Friday said the Coalition was drafting legislation to force the tax office to reverse its decision, as he called for Chalmers to be removed from his role as treasurer.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor speaking in Sydney this week. Nadir Tolj-Kinani
“The treasurer has carriage of the Australian Tax Office. I mean, seriously, just scrap it and give small businesses some breathing space right now because they don’t have it,” Taylor told News24, formerly Sky News Australia.
“This government needs to understand that small business is the backbone of our economy, the backbone of employment, the backbone of our local communities, the backbone of our country. They deserve better.”
Any such legislation by the Coalition would likely fail to pass the House of Representatives, where Labor holds a significant majority.
Several Labor MPs – speaking to this masthead on the condition of anonymity – shared concerns over the way the government’s relationship with small business was being framed, but stressed the ATO had blindsided the government and was difficult to wrangle because of its independence.
“It’s just alarming that were seeing this sort of behaviour from the ATO. It’s overreach, it’s hostile, they need to remember who they serve,” one senator said, questioning why the Reserve Bank had not foreshadowed such moves.
Another said the ATO had likely made the right decision in finding value for the taxpayer, but had botched the transition and needed to “pull its head out of the sand”.
“People probably don’t realise how completely, totally independent the tax office is of the government of the day, for good reasons, but yes, sometimes it is completely infuriating,” they said.
Concern in the Labor ranks that the party is failing to meet small business owners appears to be growing, with one particularly strident MP laying the blame directly at the feet of cabinet.
“I don’t think it’s acceptable for us to say it was the ATO’s decision not ours. If that’s the case, then there’s something seriously wrong with our government. If the ATO can dictate policy like this without government oversight and agreement, I don’t quite understand that government,” the MP said.
“I just think there is no one in cabinet with any small business experience. We have a small business minister that knows nothing about small business. We need someone with some guts to stand up to the tax office. I think it’s very, very disappointing.”
Small Business Minister Anne Aly was the first government minister to raise concerns over the ATO’s move on Wednesday, urging the tax office to consult more widely about the ban’s implementation.
